title: Bhrigu, Varuna and the chant for two
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: a father won't hand his son the answer, and a chant counts exactly two
carry: brahman isn't handed down; teacher and student seek it
tomorrow: is the sound of a chant enough, or do you need the meaning?

cards: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a young man named Bhrigu goes to his father, the god Varuna, and says: sir, teach me Brahman, the ultimate reality. Varuna doesn't give him the answer.
He gives him a pointer: that from which all beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return. Seek to know that, through tapas, discipline.
Bhrigu works, and comes back sure: it's food; everything lives by food. Varuna sends him back. Next time it's breath.
Then mind. Then understanding. Each time, back he goes.

teach.b: The same Upanishad gives teacher and student a chant to say together before study: saha navavatu, saha nau bhunaktu, saha viryam karavavahai, tejasvi navadhitam astu, ma vidvishavahai.
May it protect us two together, may it nourish us two, may we two make strength together, may our study be bright, may we two not turn against each other.
The puzzle: Sanskrit has a set of forms for exactly two people, the dual, and every verb here uses it. The chant could have said we. It says us two.
So why does the teacher pray at all? Many teachers explain it this way: the teacher doesn't own the truth and hand it down.
Teacher and student both stand in front of Brahman, which neither of them made. Varuna didn't hand Bhrigu the answer; he sent him to see it, and stayed beside him.
That's the teaching: in Hinduism, Brahman isn't handed down like a fact. A guru points, and the student has to see.
Hindus call that bond guru and shishya, teacher and student, and the chant names it before one word is taught: we two are in this together; may we not fall out. Here's where it meets now.
Priya picked this chant for the assembly. She'd planned to say it alone.
Then Sam offered to read the English beside her, and the grammar settles it: this is a prayer built for two voices, two people learning the same thing side by side, neither one above the other.

how: In traditional study, and in many Vedanta classes and schools today, teacher and student say saha navavatu together before a lesson, ending with om shanti, shanti, shanti.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: the peace treaties written in old Sanskrit between kings
a well-known prayer and the peace chants, opened up word by word
chants sung only at funerals to calm the family

games.q: a seeker, a teacher, a chant for two — tap the pairs.
p: asked his father: teach me Brahman
sent him back to seek, again and again
may we two not turn on each other

s: Varuna told Bhrigu the answer the first time he asked
he sent him back to seek, until Bhrigu saw bliss for himself.
in saha navavatu, every verb is in the dual: for exactly two
teacher and student, saying it together.
saha navavatu is said by the student alone, to the teacher
the teacher prays too: both stand before Brahman.

games.q: Priya wants the chant at the assembly and Sam offers to read the English beside her. given what the chant is, does a second voice fit?
o: no: in this chant the student prays alone to the teacher.
yes: it's a prayer for two learners together, neither above the other.
only if Sam says the Sanskrit too, word for word.
games.why: saha navavatu counts two in every verb. its home is a teacher and a student; two friends side by side echo its shape.

practice: Think of the next thing you'll learn today. Before you start, say saha navavatu, or its English, may we be protected together, with your fellow learners in mind.
If you don't pray, name one person you learn alongside and send them a line of thanks. Then sit quietly until the time runs out.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: saha navavatu, a chant in the dual, where teacher and student pray as two.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: karavavahai, may we two do; -vahai is a dual ending.

carryVoice: Keep this one: Brahman isn't handed down; teacher and student seek it together. Even the teacher prays first. See you next time.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1 (opening chant; Sanskrit, simple romanization)

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1–6 (Bhrigu asks Varuna to teach him Brahman; through tapas he finds food, breath, mind, understanding, and at last bliss)
